**Case Vignette: Mr. R.**

Mr. R. is a 54-year-old married Latin American man who presents as a parole officer in a large urban city. He has been in this role for over twenty years, having previously served as a police officer for a decade. He is soft-spoken, with a measured, deliberate way of speaking that seems to have been honed by years of navigating tense situations. He is dressed in a pressed, dark polo shirt and khakis, appearing neat and composed, though his hands are often clasped tightly in his lap.

The event that changed everything for Mr. R. occurred eighteen months ago, during a routine field operation. He was on a joint task force with local police to execute a warrant on a violent parolee. The plan was clear, the briefing thorough. But as he and two younger officers entered the apartment, a series of miscommunications and escalating shouts turned the scene chaotic. Mr. R. recalls the sound of a door slamming, a shout of “He’s got something!”, and then the percussive blast of a shotgun. He does not remember being hit, only the sensation of the floor rushing up to meet him. The shot had been fired by a rookie officer, aimed at a suspect who had reached for a cell phone, not a weapon. The buckshot caught Mr. R. in the left side of his torso and arm.

Physically, he has healed. The scars are neat, the muscle function nearly restored. But the internal landscape is a different story. In the months following, he was placed on administrative leave. He spent his days at home, sitting in the dark living room, watching the street. He stopped answering his phone. He would startle violently at the sound of a car backfiring or a child’s basketball hitting the driveway. His wife, Elena, would find him standing at the kitchen window at 3 a.m., staring out at the empty street, his breathing shallow and fast. He told her he was “just checking the perimeter.”

The most disturbing part for Mr. R. is the feeling of being a stranger in his own life. He used to be the calm center of any storm. Now, he is a storm himself. He describes a constant, low-grade static in his head, a buzzing alertness that never turns off. He has not been able to return to full duty. He was reassigned to a desk job, reviewing case files and writing reports. This is a profound humiliation for him. The job he loved—the fieldwork, the direct contact with people on the edge, the sense of making a tangible difference—is now a source of terror. The smell of a police cruiser, the crackle of a radio, the sight of a uniformed officer—any of these can trigger a visceral, full-body flashback. He will feel the phantom impact of the buckshot, smell the cordite, and hear the rookie’s panicked shouts as if they are happening in the room.

He has become profoundly avoidant. He no longer watches crime dramas on television. He has stopped attending his son’s soccer games because the crowd noise and the whistle of the referee feel like an ambush. He has withdrawn from his closest friends on the force, unable to bear their well-meaning questions or their casual talk about the job. He feels a deep, corrosive shame. He believes he should have seen it coming, should have been faster, should have prevented the mistake. He replays the seconds before the shot in his mind, searching for a different outcome.

His marriage is strained. Elena tries to be patient, but she is exhausted. He has become irritable and distant. He snapped at her last week when she accidentally dropped a metal pot in the kitchen, and he spent the next hour in a cold sweat, unable to speak. He knows he is hurting her, but he feels trapped in a glass cage of his own hypervigilance. He describes the world as feeling “thin,” like a membrane he might fall through at any moment. He lives in a state of constant, low-grade dread, waiting for the next catastrophe to find him, even when he is sitting in the safety of his own home.
